body.observations: Default r001 and X1 show the same pattern: l1 is saturated (l1_util about 1.0), UDP gets about 979 Mbps and loses about 51%, while TCP is effectively zero. E1: Cubic q4 gives tcp_goodput_bps=0, Cubic q1000 gives 5792 bps; BBR q4 gives 0, BBR q1000 gives 4634 bps. These are all far below any meaningful TCP share and differ from zero only by a few kbps. T2 shows mean l1_q=99.762376 packets in the default FIFO, i.e. the queue is persistently full. T3 shows mean tcp_cwnd=4157.623762 bytes, about 3 packets, so Cubic is not able to grow. l1_util_back=0.0 in all runs means there is no meaningful reverse ACK traffic, consistent with TCP not establishing or not getting acknowledged data. The most important unexplained fact is that neither queue length nor TCP congestion-control type can create meaningful TCP goodput when an unresponsive UDP flow offers 2 Gbps to a 1 Gbps FIFO link. The likely missing mechanism is service differentiation: FIFO gives no protected service to TCP, so TCP packets are dropped before they can be acknowledged.

body.limit: At the recommendation, TCP is limited by the scheduler's protected service share, not by TCP congestion control. With the locked greedy UDP flow and one TCP flow, the scheduler divides the 1 Gbps link between two saturated flows; E2 shows UDP 489526240 bps and TCP 482007923 bps, summing to about 971.5 Mbps payload while l1_util is 1.000001. TCP is slightly below the nominal 500 Mbps share because of packet/ACK overhead and small queueing/retransmission effects. Queue length cannot raise TCP above this share: q4 causes loss and gives 463881280 bps with 3417 retransmissions, q1000 removes TCP drops but gives only 476482765 bps, and q100 is the best tested value (E2, C4). BBR underfills the class, with mean cwnd 7597.732673 bytes versus Cubic's 137469.683168 bytes, and gets only 190096915 bps (E2, C5, T4, T5).
body.explanation: With the original FIFO queue, UDP's 2 Gbps offered load keeps the queue full (T2 mean l1_q=99.762376 packets) and TCP is starved: Cubic and BBR give 0 or only a few kbps across queue extremes (E0, E1, C1, C2). The decisive change is structural: replacing the sender-side FIFO with a scheduler queue gives TCP protected service, raising Cubic's goodput to 482007923 bps at the default queue length (E2, C3). Once that protected share exists, the knobs have the expected roles: l1.queue.length matters only through loss versus queueing delay, with q100 best among q4/q100/q1000 (E2, C4); tcp.type matters only if the TCP type fills the scheduler class. Cubic, Linux Reno, and New Reno all reach the same 482007923 bps (E2, E3, C6, C7), so the default Cubic is sufficient and simplest. BBR is worse because it keeps inflight/cwnd far below the scheduler share (E2, C5, T5).
body.holds_when: The scheduler queue change is allowed and gives the two flows comparable service; UDP remains a locked 2 Gbps greedy flow; TCP always has data; link rate, delay, MTU, and seed remain as in the brief.
body.breaks_when: If the scheduler queue is not allowed, TCP remains effectively zero under FIFO. If UDP's offered load falls below the scheduler share, TCP can exceed 482 Mbps. If the scheduler service share is weighted differently, or if untested queue lengths (for example q50/q200) or untested TCP types (for example TcpBic/TcpVegas) fill the share with less overhead, the best setting could change.

claims.text: Under the original FIFO queue, no tested queue length or tested TCP type gives meaningful TCP goodput because UDP saturation tail-drops TCP.
Replacing the sender-side FIFO queue on l1 with a scheduler queue is sufficient to give TCP meaningful goodput, about 482 Mbps with Cubic and q100.
Under the scheduler, l1.queue.length matters through loss versus queueing delay; q100 is the best tested value among q4, q100, and q1000.
Under the scheduler, loss-based TCP types Cubic, Linux Reno, and New Reno achieve the same TCP goodput, while BBR underfills the scheduler share and is much worse.
The recommended TCP rate is limited by the scheduler's protected fair share and packet/ACK overhead, not by the choice among loss-based TCP types.

open_questions: Whether untested queue lengths such as q50 or q200 could improve TCP goodput by more than 1% over q100.
Whether untested TCP types TcpBic or TcpVegas could match or exceed the scheduler-limited 482 Mbps.
The exact breakdown of the gap between TCP's 482.0 Mbps and the nominal 500 Mbps scheduler share into header overhead, ACK effects, queueing, and retransmissions.
